\chapter{Para --- For, Pointing Forward}
\label{ch:para}
\hlchaptermodality{154}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use para for a destination, a deadline, a recipient or a purpose.}

Complete ES-C51-para: produce para ti and para manana, and name the Latin piece inside para that means toward.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[para]{para — \textquotedblleft{}for,\textquotedblright{} pointing forward}

\label{lesson:ES-C51-para}



\begin{quote}
English has one word, \emph{for}, doing about ten jobs. Spanish splits them between two words, and most courses hand you a list of twelve rules. You are getting one idea instead, and this chapter is half of it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the arrow points away from you}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{para} — \emph{for}, when something is \textbf{aimed at} something else.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Es \textbf{para} ti.} — It's for you. \emph{(aimed at a person)} \emph{\textbf{Para} mañana.} — By tomorrow. \emph{(aimed at a moment)} \emph{Hago la comida \textbf{para} la casa.} — I make the meal for the house. \emph{(aimed at a purpose)}
\end{quote}

Destination, deadline, recipient, purpose. They look like four different rules and they are one: \textbf{something is heading toward something else.} Draw an arrow from the thing to its target, and if the arrow makes sense, the word is \emph{para}.

That is the whole of this chapter. Not four uses — one direction.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
The direction is not a mnemonic somebody invented. It is \textbf{inside the word}.

\emph{Para} was Latin \textbf{per} + \textbf{ad}, squeezed into one word. And \emph{ad} means \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}toward\textquotedblright{}} — it is the same \emph{ad} sitting at the front of English \textbf{advance}, \textbf{admit}, \textbf{adhere}, \textbf{address}, all of which are about moving or pointing at something.

So \emph{para} is, at the bottom, \textquotedblleft{}through-toward.\textquotedblright{} A word that is literally made of an arrow.

Once you have that, you do not have to remember which of the twelve textbook uses of \emph{para} is which. You have to ask one question: \textbf{is this pointing at something?}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}para ti\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}para mañana\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}para la casa\textquotedblright{} — draw the arrow each time
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What one question decides \emph{para}? (\textbf{Is it pointing at something?}) What is inside the word? (\emph{\textbf{Ad}} — \textquotedblleft{}toward.\textquotedblright{}) Next: the other half — and you have been saying it since your first chapter.
\end{tcolorbox}
